submission.natural_language_explanation: N521+ fires on the predicate word of a clause - the verb, predicative adjective or focused adverb that carries the assertion - and a subordinating opener multiplies its strength several-fold: 'if you want' 0.75 vs 'So you want' 0.00, 'when you want' 0.58 vs 'while you want' 0.10, 'whether you want' 0.65 vs 'although you want' 0.11, 'if I did' 1.13 vs 'since I did' 0.67, 'if you have questions' 1.34 vs the same without 'if' 0.62, 'until now' 1.06 vs 'until then' 0.77, against 0.0-0.2 for the subordinator itself, for determiners/prepositions/auxiliaries, for later content words of the same clause ('if you want to make shopping economic': 'make'/'shopping'/'economic' all 0.00), for ordinary noun objects in plain declaratives ('He bought the hat/lawyer/car yesterday' 0.00), and for the same verb when the clause opens with So/And/While/Although/After (0.00-0.10). Without any subordinator it still fires at 0.4-1.4 on a small intrinsic-propensity set of predicate words ('had been dominant' 1.16, 'is critical' 0.97, 'particularly difficult' 1.23, 'In return' 0.78), so its strongest peaks need both factors.

rival_explanations: A pure token-identity detector: the pole fires on a fixed lexical list (could, only, want, did, questions, now, critical, dominant) wherever those words occur, and 'if' merely happens to appear beside them in the scan's top examples - it predicts 'So you want to help' fires as hard as 'If you want to help' (measured 0.00 vs 0.75).

A broad content-word detector: any noun, verb or adjective drives the pole in proportion to how informative the model finds it, with no clause-level gating - it predicts 'He bought the hat yesterday' and 'if you want to make shopping economic' light up the object and the later verbs (measured 0.00 for all of them).

A non-Latin byte-fallback detector: its strongest single token is ' �' and four of twenty top examples are broken Greek byte fragments, so the English clause examples would be a weak offshoot and any byte-split out-of-vocabulary token would fire it at full strength.

top_examples.text:
THROWBACK- Founder of the ACLU: “Communism is the Goal”

Freedom oriented individuals should always be wary of an organization that is left-leaning, and for good reason. While once in a while organizations such as the ACLU appear to be doing some good work that we can get behind, its goals always bring their work into question.

This is especially true of organizations such as Planned Parenthood, whose founder, Margaret Sanger, started the institution with the goal of eradicating African Americans. Or organizations like MoveOn, which is funded by George Soros, who “admittedly enjoys collapsing the governments and economies of sovereign nations and, in fact, finds it ‘fun.'”

The same questions must also be asked of the American Civil Liberties Union. The ACLU seems innocuous in their advocacy of civil liberties, but their selective fight for left-wing issues brings its goals into question. They are ardent defenders of demographics which vote Democrat, yet have pushed to censor prayer in school, and have fought tooth and nail against the Boy Scouts for referencing God in their oath, among other things.

The ACLU’s leftist agenda perhaps becomes more clear when you look to the words of one of its founders, Roger Nash Baldwin, who said in 1935:

“I am for socialism, disarmament, and, ultimately, for abolishing the state itself… I seek the social ownership of property, the abolition of the propertied class, and the sole control of those who produce wealth. Communism is the goal.”

In fact just four years prior to Baldwin’s quote, while investigating communist activities within the US, a Special House Committee concluded that:

“The American Civil Liberties Union is closely affiliated with the communist movement in the United States, and fully 90 percent of its efforts are on behalf of communists who have come into conflict with the law. It claims to stand for free speech, free press and free assembly, but it is quite apparent that the main function of the ACLU is an attempt to protect the communists.”

Baldwin did change his views on communism later in his life, and allegedly kicked all members of the Communist Party off of the ACLU board. But the organization’s founding and continued promotion of a left-wing agenda should be enough to get any reasonable American to question its goals.

London, January 26 (ANI): Genes chemically silenced by stress during life remain silenced in eggs and sperm, allowing the effect to be passed down to the next generation, researchers say.
Obtained from detailed DNA scans in developing mouse eggs and sperm, the finding backs up mounting indirect proof from statistical studies that the genetic impacts of environmental factors like smoking, diet, stressed childhoods, famine and psychiatric disease can be passed down to future generations through a process called epigenetic inheritance.
Many geneticists had considered this impossible.
Genes can be switched off by changing DNA through a chemical process called methylation, in which enzymes respond to environmental factors by marking genes with methyl groups that prevent them from working.
However, the idea that genes carrying these epigenetic markings could be inherited is controversial.
A team of researchers led by Jamie Hackett from the University of Cambridge has challenged the findings of the previous studies.
According to previous studies, as sperm and eggs develop any markings added to genes during life are erased to provide a genetic blank slate from which the next generation develops.
Any remaining marks were also thought to be wiped out when an egg is fertilised.
For the current study, the extracted the DNA from mouse primordial germ cells - the precursors to sperm and eggs - at various stages of their development and used markers to spot any methylated genes.
They found that a tiny number of methylated gene regions survived unerased: an average of just 233 out of approximately 25,000 in the germ cells examined.
Still, the work clearly shows that traits resulting from the surviving markings can potentially be passed on.
"What we've found is a potential way things can get through, whereas before, everything was considered to be erased," News Scientist quoted Hackett as saying. (ANI)

One of the bigger evolutions in education has been the push to get kids to become more computer-literate, yet one of the hardest hurdles has been making the process of learning and writing programming languages less dry. A startup out of southern California has found an innovative way of tackling this, using a golfball-sized robot that follows trails that you draw using fat, colored felt tip markers, or the equivalent traced out on a tablet screen — or both.
Ozobot, as the robot is called, made a popular debut last year at CES. After its first sales run over the most recent holiday period ($50 per Ozobot, which includes some games, apps and other software to use it) and a number of educational endorsements from the likes of the Boys and Girls Club, Boy Scouts National STEM initiative and SAS Curriculum Pathways, Ozobot maker Evollve is introducing a new verion of the product that will let you use Blockly, Google’s library for building visual programming editors, to write out commands for the Ozobot.
The new version will come out later this year.
The magic of Ozobot is that it’s very simple to get it to work right — thereby drawing in users quickly and encouraging them to try to do more. The tiny Ozobot robots — which work now on iOS and Android and potentially Microsoft later this year — move by following lines that you have drawn either on a piece of paper or on a screen, and you can customise what they do by changing the colors of the lines. Some of the current options for actions include getting the Ozobot to spin in a circle, or speed up (turbo charge).
This is where the coding aspect comes in: right now you can “program” the robot to move using the software that comes with the Ozobot robots. Later will come Blockly. And longer term, the company tells me that the plan is to open up Ozobot’s controls to work with a variety of computing languages. The aim, for now, isn’t so much to teach programming languages like Python or C++, but to get younger people into the mindset of how to conceive of a sequence of commands and attach them to a visual outcome.
There is a social element to this one, too. “Kids have become too solitary, and so we have really tried to focus on something in the physical world with Ozobot,” CEO and founder Nader Hamda told me.
A lot of computer games are made for the pure enjoyment of gameplay, but as Minecraft has shown, sometimes that can lead to another side-effect, where fun gets repurposed as a platform to teach coding and computational mechanics.
Ozobot has taken a slightly different approach: it has built an educational aim directly into the original purpose of the product, while still trying to make it fun and usable by those who simply want to conceive of games using the basic building blocks of a tiny robot and customizable, squiggly lines.
Evollve has raised several million dollars in funding from a selection of angels and is now beginning talks with institutional VCs, Hamda tells me.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The mechanic explained that the old truck could be repaired by Friday, and he promised to call again.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' could' is a modal auxiliary in an unsubordinated declarative whose predicates are off the intrinsic-propensity set, so the hypothesis predicts near-zero while a token-list reading predicts a hit.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She only had three dollars left in her purse, so she walked home through the rain.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' only' sits as a bare focus adverb with no subordinating opener, the configuration the hypothesis says is not enough to fire; only the token-identity rival predicts a hit.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: There was a want of decent housing in the town, and the council knew it.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Keeps ' want' but as a noun rather than the clause predicate and with no subordinator; the hypothesis names ordinary noun objects in plain declaratives as non-firing, so it predicts silence while a token-identity reading predicts firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Although you want the roof repaired before winter, the landlord will delay it until spring.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Direct test of the hypothesis's own Although/whether split: ' want' heads a subordinate clause opened by 'Although' (0.11) rather than 'whether' (0.65), so it predicts no fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: After I did the dishes and swept the floor, the kitchen looked tidy enough.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Direct test of the After/If split on ' did': the hypothesis reports 0.00-0.10 for clauses opened by 'After' against 1.13 for 'if I did'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: While you want the meeting moved to Thursday, the rest of the team prefers Friday morning.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Direct test of the While/When split (0.10 versus 0.58), keeping ' want' and a clause-level opener and swapping only the opener's identity.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: And the supervisor could hardly believe the speed of the new interns in their first week.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' could' follows a clause-initial 'And', one of the coordinating openers the hypothesis measures at 0.00-0.10, so it predicts no fire despite the trigger token.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Martha bought a lamp at the flea market, carried it home and set it by the window.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A plain declarative whose nouns and verbs are all off the intrinsic-propensity set, predicted silent by the hypothesis (as with its 'bought the hat' measurement) but active by a broad content-word detector.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: If in doubt about the wiring, ask an electrician to inspect it before the winter.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'if' opens a verbless phrase so no predicate word is available to carry the assertion, and the main-clause verbs are off the intrinsic set, so the hypothesis predicts no fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The foreman shrugged, wiped his greasy hands and told the crew they could finish the fence by noon.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' could' sits in an unsubordinated complement clause with no subordinating opener, testing that the hypothesis needs the opener and not merely an auxiliary further into the sentence.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The reporter asked several pointed questions about the budget, and the mayor ended the briefing early.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Keeps the trigger ' questions' as a plural noun object of an ordinary verb with no subordinator, a role the hypothesis names as non-firing, while both the token-list and the content-word rivals predict firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: From now on the office closes at five, and the mail room shuts at four.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' now' appears as a bare temporal adverb with no 'until' opener, which the hypothesis says is not enough for its peak; only a token-identity reading predicts firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The difficult climb along the ridge exhausted the hikers, and the guide called for a rest.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Keeps ' difficult' as an attributive modifier inside a noun phrase rather than the predicative adjective the hypothesis names ('particularly difficult' 1.23), and the clause's main verb is off the intrinsic set, so it predicts no fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The dominant theme of the lecture was patience, and the students scribbled notes in the margins.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Keeps ' dominant' attributively in a noun phrase rather than as the clause predicate ('had been dominant' 1.16), testing whether predication or mere token identity drives the pole.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Every critical remark in the review deserved an answer, and the manager drafted one slowly.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Keeps ' critical' as a prenominal modifier in no predicative or subordinated position, so the hypothesis predicts silence while a content-word or token-list reading predicts firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The fund reported a modest return on its investments, and the clerk filed the paperwork quickly.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Keeps ' return' as a noun object in a plain prepositional phrase, unlike the hypothesis's intrinsic-set 'In return' (0.78), so the hypothesis predicts no fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Πληθυσμός 210 κάτοικοι, υψόμετρο 340 μέτρα, επαρχία Λευκωσίας.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A verbless Greek infobox fragment; the model renders it with raw-byte ' �' tokens, exactly what the byte-fallback rival says fires at full strength, while the hypothesis, an English clause-predicate claim, predicts nothing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Aunque quieres el coche nuevo, el taller tarda dos semanas en arreglar el viejo.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A Spanish near-miss of 'Although you want' in the same script: subordinate opener plus assertion-carrying verb, which the hypothesis's English-only intrinsic set and its own Although measurement predict is silent; the split is ordinary Latin BPE, with no raw-byte ' �' token, so the non-Latin byte-fallback rival does not engage.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: So you want the keys to the van, and the insurance papers as well.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The hypothesis's own contrast case: 'So you want' measured 0.00 against 'if you want' 0.75, so it predicts no fire even though every trigger token is present.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The crew loaded the van before sunrise, checked the tyres and the lights, and the driver said they could reach the northern depot by noon; the gateman waved them through and nobody asked any questions.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A long unsubordinated passage carrying both ' could' and ' questions' with no subordinating opener anywhere, so the hypothesis predicts silence at every position while a token-list reading predicts firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: If you want to help with the harvest, come to the barn at dawn on Saturday.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Paraphrase holdout of the hypothesis's strongest case, 'if you want', in a new rural context unlike the scanned examples.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: When you want the room quiet, close the shutters and turn off the ceiling fan.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests 'when you want' (0.58) in a new imperative context, the positive counterpart of the 'While you want' negative.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Whether you want a single room or a suite, the clerk will find something for you.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests 'whether you want' (0.65) in a hotel context, the positive counterpart of the 'Although you want' negative.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: If I did something to upset her, she never said a word about it at the time.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests 'if I did' (1.13) in a new first-person context, the positive counterpart of the 'After I did' negative.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: If you have questions about the new schedule, please write to the office before Friday noon.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests 'if you have questions' (1.34) in a workplace context, the positive counterpart of the 'questions'-as-object negative.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Until now the ferry has run only in summer, but the town wants a winter service too.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests 'until now' (1.06, against 0.77 for 'until then') in a transport context, the positive counterpart of the bare-'now' negative.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Their early results had been dominant for a decade, and the reviewers took note.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests the subordinator-free intrinsic-propensity case 'had been dominant' (1.16) in a new context, the positive counterpart of the attributive-'dominant' negative.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: If the delivery of floor tiles from the depot near the old harbour finally arrives before the inspectors leave on Friday, the foreman will sign the papers.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Paraphrase holdout with none of the claimed trigger tokens, where 'if' opens the clause and the assertion-carrying verb 'arrives' sits about fifteen tokens away, testing both the subordinator claim and its long-range reach.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Whenever the morning shipment arrives late, the manager calls the depot to complain about it.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Paraphrase holdout with none of the claimed trigger tokens: a 'whenever' subordinator plus an assertion-carrying verb, which the hypothesis predicts fires but a token-identity detector predicts is silent.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: // If you want the cache cleared, restart the service after the migration finishes.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Cross-genre holdout (a code comment) of 'if you want' (0.75), testing that the subordinator-plus-predicate claim survives outside prose.

readings.explanation: N521+ fires on the predicate word of a clause - the verb, predicative adjective or focused adverb that carries the assertion - and a subordinating opener multiplies its strength several-fold: 'if you want' 0.75 vs 'So you want' 0.00, 'when you want' 0.58 vs 'while you want' 0.10, 'whether you want' 0.65 vs 'although you want' 0.11, 'if I did' 1.13 vs 'since I did' 0.67, 'if you have questions' 1.34 vs the same without 'if' 0.62, 'until now' 1.06 vs 'until then' 0.77, against 0.0-0.2 for the subordinator itself, for determiners/prepositions/auxiliaries, for later content words of the same clause ('if you want to make shopping economic': 'make'/'shopping'/'economic' all 0.00), for ordinary noun objects in plain declaratives ('He bought the hat/lawyer/car yesterday' 0.00), and for the same verb when the clause opens with So/And/While/Although/After (0.00-0.10). Without any subordinator it still fires at 0.4-1.4 on a small intrinsic-propensity set of predicate words ('had been dominant' 1.16, 'is critical' 0.97, 'particularly difficult' 1.23, 'In return' 0.78), so its strongest peaks need both factors.

A pure token-identity detector: the pole fires on a fixed lexical list (could, only, want, did, questions, now, critical, dominant) wherever those words occur, and 'if' merely happens to appear beside them in the scan's top examples - it predicts 'So you want to help' fires as hard as 'If you want to help' (measured 0.00 vs 0.75).

A broad content-word detector: any noun, verb or adjective drives the pole in proportion to how informative the model finds it, with no clause-level gating - it predicts 'He bought the hat yesterday' and 'if you want to make shopping economic' light up the object and the later verbs (measured 0.00 for all of them).

A non-Latin byte-fallback detector: its strongest single token is ' �' and four of twenty top examples are broken Greek byte fragments, so the English clause examples would be a weak offshoot and any byte-split out-of-vocabulary token would fire it at full strength.
